Who is David Imon, Chittagong's alleged underworld figure?
item.description:
After months of investigation, law enforcement agencies on Wednesday arrested alleged Chittagong crime figure Mobarak Hossain Imon, widely known as David Imon, in Jessore following what police described as an intelligence-led operation.
Jessore Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime) Mirajul Islam confirmed the arrest to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday afternoon.
Police allege that Imon was a key figure in an extortion network targeting businesses across Chittagong, demanding a one-time payment of Tk2 crore along with Tk10 lakh every month. Authorities say his arrest followed months of coordinated efforts by intelligence and law enforcement agencies across the country.
Earlier this month, a video allegedly linked to Imon's extortion demands went viral on social media. Several audio and video recordings containing alleged death threats and extortion demands also circulated widely online, triggering public concern and intensifying pressure on law enforcement agencies to arrest him.
A team from the Chittagong District Police arrested Imon along with five associates, all of whom police allege are armed shooters. Investigators say Imon has gained notoriety over the past two years in connection with multiple extortion, intimidation and violent crime cases.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday evening, Chittagong District Police Superintendent Masud Alam said Imon is an accused in at least 15 criminal cases and is believed to be a close associate of fugitive crime figure Sajjad Ali, also known as Boro Sajjad, who police say is currently living abroad.
"Imon is being questioned, and we expect to recover important evidence. He is accused in several cases involving extortion, murder and other serious crimes. Legal proceedings will proceed in accordance with the law," Masud Alam said.
He added that police would brief the media on the case at a press conference scheduled for Thursday morning.
According to police, Boro Sajjad's criminal network consists of around 50 armed associates and shooters. Investigators allege that Imon and another associate, Mohammad Raihan, regularly collected extortion on Sajjad's behalf while Sajjad directed operations from abroad.
Mobarak Hossain Imon is the son of Md Musa of Kanchannagar in Fatikchhari upazila of Chittagong.
According to police records, he is an accused in at least 15 criminal cases, including the March 30, 2025 Bakalia double murder case and the May 23, 2025 murder of alleged criminal Dhakaiya Akbar near Patenga Sea Beach.
Police claim Imon had access to between 15 and 20 firearms and was skilled in using weapons. Investigators also allege that he arranged armed criminals and motorcycles used in the Bakalia double murder.
Senior police officials say that after Sajjad Hossain, also known as Chhoto Sajjad, was imprisoned, leadership of the criminal network in Chittagong shifted to Imon and Mohammad Raihan.
Investigators say an audio recording that went viral on social media on January 26 captured Imon allegedly threatening a man named Aziz Uddin.
"Even if you have 50,000 police guarding you, I'll come to your house and kill you. Just as I shot your brother in front of 10,000 people."
On May 10, Imon allegedly threatened journalist Biplob Dey Partha, demanding Tk50 lakh and warning that he would be shot within 24 hours if the money was not paid. The journalist later filed a General Diary (GD) with Kotwali Police Station.
Police also allege that on July 13, Imon led an attack on the office of internet service provider Digital Dot Net (DDN) on the Chandanpura-Bakalia Access Road in Chittagong. Investigators say that after failing to secure an extortion payment of Tk2 crore, the attackers vandalized the office and looted Tk35 lakh. Video footage of the attack later spread widely on social media.
According to investigators, two days before the attack Imon called businessman Adil Bin Mamun from a foreign phone number and allegedly said:
"If you want to do business, you must pay Tk2 crore upfront and Tk10 lakh every month. From now on, we will control the business."
Imon's arrest has been welcomed by many residents and business owners in Chittagong, several of whom said they hoped it would help curb extortion and organized crime in the city.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Chittagong resident Shamsuddin Ilias said the viral videos had created widespread panic among residents. He said many other dangerous criminals remain active and urged authorities to bring not only the criminals but also their patrons to justice in order to dismantle organized criminal networks.
"I had heard many times that he would be arrested. Finally, it has happened, and that itself is a relief," he said.
Businessman Adil Bin Mamun, who claims to be one of the victims of the alleged extortion, said business owners had been living in constant fear because of Imon's activities.
"We have been living in fear because of these threats. I hope this arrest allows us to run our businesses safely again and sends a strong message to others involved in extortion," he said.

item.title: Tree fair gains momentum in Khulna
item.description:
The month-long tree fair at Khulna Circuit House Ground is drawing large crowds as visitors flock to explore a wide range of local and exotic plant varieties.
Organised jointly by the Khulna district administration and the Sundarban West Forest Department, the fair began on July 11 to promote tree plantation and raise environmental awareness, particularly among younger people.
According to the fair's control room, 62 organisations, including 10 government agencies, are participating in this year's event. The fair remains open daily from 9am with free entry.
As of Monday, around 37,570 saplings worth Tk 54,27,620 had been sold, reflecting strong public interest.
Rare and exotic saplings have emerged as major attractions, including the medicinal Corossol Tree, believed to have cancer-preventive properties, the Ghugu Pakhi variety and Star Jui, which is priced at Tk15,000 per plant.
Fruit trees, particularly mango saplings, are among the best-selling items, while urban gardeners are showing growing interest in dwarf and early-fruiting varieties suitable for rooftops and small spaces. Flowering plants, orchids and tub-friendly fruit plants are also in high demand.
"The price of fruit plants that bear year-round ranges from Tk800 to Tk1,500," said Abu Masud, owner of Dalia Nursery. He said his stall features a range of fruit plants aimed at urban gardeners, alongside moringa saplings grown from seeds sourced from India.
Visitors said they came to expand their rooftop gardens with fruit and ornamental plants.
"I bought a moringa plant, a Japanese cherry blossom plant and several varieties of roses," said Sithi Islam, a resident of Nirala.
Farzana Mithila of Hazi Mohsin Road said she purchased fruit and flower plants, along with three lojjaboti saplings.
Md Zakir Hossain, duty officer at the fair's control room, said adequate security measures had been put in place for traders and visitors.
The annual fair has been a popular event in Khulna for nearly a decade, attracting nature lovers and gardening enthusiasts from across the city.

item.title: Bumper harvest, fair prices lift Rajshahi jute growers
item.description:
After years of low returns and rising production costs, jute farmers in Rajshahi are finally seeing a turnaround as strong prices and a bumper harvest breathe new life into the country's traditional ‘golden fibre.’
Freshly harvested jute is selling for Tk4,000-4,500 per maund, up sharply from Tk3,000-3,500 at the start of last season, allowing growers to recover costs comfortably and earn healthy profits.
The improved market has also fuelled optimism that jute could reclaim its position as one of the country's most profitable cash crops if prices remain stable throughout the harvesting season.
At Nowhata Haat in Paba upazila on Monday, trading was brisk as farmers arrived with freshly processed fibre loaded onto vans, three-wheelers and locally made Nosimon vehicles.
Bablu Ahmed of Choubaria village, who cultivated an early jute variety on five bighas, said he harvested around 11 maunds per bigha and sold part of his produce at Tk4,500 per maund.
"After covering production costs, I'm expecting a profit of around Tk25,000 per bigha," he said.
Abdul Alim of Bargachhi Union said he spent nearly Tk22,000 to cultivate each bigha of land this season. With favourable weather producing yields of 10-12 maunds per bigha, he expects to earn around Tk20,000 in profit per bigha.
Traders also reported a much stronger market than last year.
"Last season we bought jute for Tk3,000 to Tk3,500 per maund. This year we're paying around Tk4,500, and even more for premium-quality fibre," said trader Janip Hossain of Nowhata Bazar.
Across Paba, farmers are simultaneously harvesting jute and preparing fields for Aman paddy transplantation. While encouraged by the current prices, many remain wary that rates could fall once peak-season supplies enter the market.
They also cited labour shortages and inadequate water bodies for retting, forcing them to transport harvested jute over long distances and increasing production costs.
According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), jute cultivation in Rajshahi has expanded to 18,399 hectares this season, up from 17,305 hectares last year. The district has set a production target of 49,333 metric tonnes, compared with 48,677 metric tonnes produced last year.
Rajshahi DAE Deputy Director Mohammad Nasir Uddin said the crop initially faced setbacks due to drought and a diesel shortage. However, timely rainfall, improved fuel supplies and proper crop management helped farmers achieve good yields.
"The current market price is encouraging. Farmers are expected to make better profits this year, which will have a positive impact on the rural economy," he said.
Paba Upazila Agriculture Officer MA Mannan said sustained prices throughout the season could encourage more farmers to expand jute cultivation next year.
Meanwhile, Assistant Director of the Department of Jute in Rajshahi Md Nadim Akhtar said production is projected to reach 381,696 quintals this year, up from 360,494 quintals last year.
He said the combination of higher output and favourable prices has created fresh optimism among growers, who believe a stable market could help restore jute's importance in Bangladesh's agricultural economy.

item.title: DU to review 15 years of appointments, investigate teachers over July uprising
item.description:
Dhaka University's (DU) Syndicate has decided to review all appointments of teachers, officers and staff made between January 1, 2009, and June 30, 2024, while also launching an investigation into allegations against teachers accused of opposing students during the July 2024 mass uprising.
The decisions were taken at a Syndicate meeting on Tuesday, chaired by Vice-Chancellor Prof ABM Obaidul Islam, who confirmed them to Dhaka Tribune.
To review appointments made during the period, the Syndicate formed an investigation committee headed by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Academic) Prof Abdus Salam. Deans of the university's various faculties will serve as members of the committee.
The Syndicate also decided to review research activities carried out under the World Bank- and University Grants Commission (UGC)-funded Higher Education Quality Enhancement Project (HEQEP) during the same period to determine whether project funds were properly utilised.
A separate committee, headed by Pro-Vice-Chancellor (Administration) Prof Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane, has been formed to conduct the review.
The Syndicate also constituted a four-member committee to investigate allegations against teachers accused of taking a stand against students during the July 2024 mass uprising.
The committee comprises the vice-chancellor, the two pro-vice-chancellors and Syndicate member Prof Morshed Hasan Khan. It will examine a list of 125 teachers submitted by the platform Dhaka Bisshobiddyaloyer Fyasibad-birodhi Shikkhok-mondoli to determine whether they opposed students during the uprising.
According to the decisions taken at the meeting, if any accused teacher is found to be affiliated with a teachers' organization, action may also be taken against that organization.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Alfasane said a list had been submitted naming teachers accused of being aligned with forces that opposed the 2024 mass uprising.
He said that if the committee's investigation finds any teacher responsible, disciplinary action will be taken. If any organization is found to have been involved, action will also be taken against it.
"The committee will thoroughly examine the video footage, photographs and news reports submitted as evidence before identifying those responsible and recommending appropriate measures. If any organization is found to be involved, we will take action against it as well," he said.
Meanwhile, activists from Ducsu, hall unions and Islami Chhatra Shibir demonstrated outside the Syndicate meeting, alleging that it was preparing to approve a revised hall seat-allocation policy that would allow irregular students to stay in university residence halls for an additional year.
The protesters used a handheld microphone outside the venue, with the sound reportedly carrying into the meeting hall.
Amid the protests, the proposed policy was not approved.
The vice-chancellor said a final decision would be taken after further discussions with the relevant stakeholders.
He also said the university would review footage of those who used the handheld microphone outside the venue to project sound into the meeting hall.
The Syndicate also imposed disciplinary measures of varying severity and duration against several teachers over separate allegations. Those include Prof Md Abdul Muhit of the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology, Prof Abu Sara Shamsur Rouf of the Department of Pharmaceutical Technology, Prof Mohammad Bahauddin of the Department of Persian Language and Literature, Dr Rafiq Shahriar (Rafiqul Islam) of the Department of Peace and Conflict Studies, Prof Afroza Shelley of the Department of Nuclear Engineering and Prof Md Shafiqul Islam.

He replaced Mehidy Hasan Miraz as captain in this format.
In doing so, the board gave Liton the responsibility to lead the side in two formats of white-ball cricket. He has already been leading the side in T20 format.
Najmul Hossain Shanto continues leading the side in Test cricket.
Tamim said the board had approved the decision as they believe the arrangement would better serve the team's long-term interests.
Towhid Hridoy has been named the white-ball vice-captain, while the red-ball vice-captain will remain unchanged.
Explaining the decision to relieve Mehidy Hasan Miraz of the captaincy, Tamim praised his leadership but said the all-rounder was needed more as a performer.
"Miraz has done an excellent job as captain in recent series, but we want him to focus fully on his batting and bowling and return to the level we expect from him," Tamim said, adding that the decision was taken after discussions with the player and with mutual consent.
He also indicated that Miraz could return to a leadership role in the future, citing his significant contribution to Bangladesh cricket.
Tamim said injury management was a major factor behind opting against three different captains across the formats.
He revealed that the growing number of injuries among the country's fast bowlers had made workload management increasingly important.
"When there are three captains, each wants to field the best bowlers in his format, which puts extra pressure on the players. With separate white-ball and red-ball captains, they can coordinate better and manage workloads more effectively," he said.
Tamim informed that following Bangladesh's recent tour of Zimbabwe, he met with the coaching staff and players to formulate a six-month roadmap aimed at improving the national team's performances.

item.title: Alleged top criminal David Emon arrested in Jessore
item.description:
Detective Branch (DB) police on Wednesday arrested alleged top criminal Mobarak Hossain Emon, also known as David Emon, in Jessore.
Jessore Additional Superintendent of Police (Crime) Mirajul Islam confirmed the arrest to Dhaka Tribune at around 2pm.
"DB police arrested David Emon from a vehicle in the Jhumjhumpur area on the Jessore-Narail Highway. He is now in the custody of Jessore police. Details will be provided later," he said.
According to police, Emon and Mohammad Raihan allegedly took over leadership of a criminal syndicate in Chittagong after the arrest of Chhoto Sajjad, an alleged associate of fugitive criminal Sajjad Ali Khan. Investigators alleged that Chhoto Sajjad had previously carried out criminal activities on behalf of Boro Sajjad.
Police said followers of Sajjad Ali Khan have been behind most recent extortion demands and attacks in Chittagong city and the upazilas of Raozan, Hathazari and Fatikchhari. Law enforcement agencies had been searching for both Emon and Raihan before Wednesday's arrest.
One of the cases linked to Emon is an alleged extortion attempt targeting Digital Dot Net (DDN), a Chittagong-based business.
According to police, DDN owner Adil Bin Mamun received a call from a foreign number on July 11 from a person identifying himself as David Emon, who allegedly demanded Tk20 million in extortion and threatened further attacks if the money was not paid.
Police said that two days later, at around 12:30pm on July 13, about 30 to 35 armed men attacked the DDN office on the Chandanpura-Bakalia Access Road under Chawkbazar Police Station.
The assailants allegedly vandalized the office, looted Tk3.5 million kept there for salary payments and warned the company against continuing its operations. CCTV footage of the attack later circulated on social media.
Police said the attacked office is adjacent to the residence of Smart Group Director Mujibur Rahman, where gunfire was reported on February 28 while the house was under police protection. Investigators alleged that followers of fugitive criminal Sajjad Ali Khan carried out the attack after failing to extort money from the businessman.
The same residence also came under gunfire on January 2, when bullets struck its windows and doors. Police protection remained in place following the incident.
Earlier, Chittagong police arrested two alleged associates of Emon from the Wazedia area on the Oxygen-Kuaish Road, recovering a foreign-made pistol and four rounds of ammunition.
The suspects, identified as Md Asif, 25, and Saidul Islam, alias Arif, 24, were arrested on Sunday night. Police said Asif was a fugitive accused in a criminal case.

item.title: Dhaka buries canals, now monsoon buries its roads
item.description:
Dhaka’s recurring monsoon paralysis is not simply the result of excessive rainfall but the consequence of decades spent filling, narrowing and polluting the canals that once carried stormwater out of the capital.
An investigation by Dhaka Tribune found that many waterways still shown on official maps have either vanished beneath buildings, roads and markets or been reduced to narrow, waste-choked drains incapable of performing their natural function.
Once connected to the Buriganga, Turag, Balu and Shitalakkhya rivers, Dhaka’s canal network formed the backbone of its drainage system.
Rainwater flowed through the canals into the surrounding rivers, while wetlands absorbed excess runoff and helped maintain the city’s ecological balance.
Much of that system has now been destroyed.
The consequences emerge with every monsoon shower.
Roads disappear beneath murky water, traffic comes to a standstill, businesses close and thousands of commuters become stranded after only a few hours of rain.
Neighbourhoods including Mirpur, Kalshi, Mohammadpur, Badda, Aftabnagar, Banasree, Rampura, Jatrabari, Demra and parts of Old Dhaka now experience prolonged waterlogging even after moderate rainfall.
Experts say Dhaka has effectively built over the routes through which water once escaped.
Decades of unplanned urbanisation, weak enforcement, institutional conflict and politically protected encroachment have transformed the city’s natural drainage assets into one of its greatest urban liabilities.
Some canals have been filled to make way for multistorey buildings.
Others have been occupied by roads, markets, commercial structures and informal settlements.
Box culverts have buried waterways underground, while household sewage, plastic waste and construction debris have obstructed those that remain exposed.
The result is a city increasingly unable to drain itself.
Responsibility for the canals has shifted repeatedly without halting their decline.
In 1988, the government handed 26 canals to Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority to improve the capital’s drainage system.
They remained under Wasa’s management for more than three decades, during which encroachment continued and several canals gradually disappeared.
Canal management was transferred to Dhaka North and South city corporations in 2021 amid hopes that local authorities would recover the waterways and improve drainage.
Residents and urban planners say little has fundamentally changed.
A senior Wasa official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the agency’s drainage infrastructure had originally been designed to carry stormwater and wastewater, but thousands of illegal sewage connections had overwhelmed it.
“Our drains were never designed to receive untreated waste directly from thousands of buildings,” the official said.
“Developers, poor enforcement and the lack of proper coordination allowed sewage to flow into the drainage network. The canals eventually became clogged.”
The official said responsibility should be shared among Wasa, Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha, or Rajuk, and both city corporations.
Field visits to Nandipara, Manda, Mugda, Shonir Akhra and Mohammadpur revealed household sewage pipes discharging directly into canals.
Plastic, domestic rubbish and construction waste floated on stagnant black water or formed barriers that restricted its movement.
In several places, the canals had become open sewers, emitting a strong odour and creating breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
Alamgir Hossain, a Rampura resident, recalled when the neighbourhood canal still carried clean water.
“Now it has become a dumping ground. The smell is unbearable,” he said.
“Illegal structures have occupied both sides, and in many places it has become nothing more than a drain.”
Mohammad Shahjahan, who grew up in Hatirpool, said the area’s canal had disappeared completely beneath urban development.
“When we were children, there was an actual canal here,” he said. “Today, everything has been replaced by buildings.”
The lost canal at Hatirpool is one example of a broader transformation in which the physical traces of Dhaka’s waterways have disappeared while their names remain embedded in the city’s neighbourhoods and roads.
Public money has continued to flow into restoration projects, but questions remain over their impact.
In October 2022, the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council approved a project costing approximately Tk898.73 crore to restore the Kalunagar, Jirani, Manda and Shyampur canals.
Implemented by Dhaka South City Corporation, the project aimed to restore water flow, reduce waterlogging and develop walkways, cycling lanes, playgrounds, green spaces and recreational facilities.
It was scheduled for completion by June 2026.
However, site visits found many sections still polluted, encroached upon or unable to function effectively as drainage channels.
Urban planners say beautification will achieve little unless authorities first restore the canals’ width, depth, continuity and connections to surrounding rivers.
Professor Adil Muhammad Khan of Jahangirnagar University’s Department of Urban and Regional Planning said Dhaka’s waterlogging was fundamentally a planning failure.
“Canals are the primary pathways through which rainwater reaches rivers,” he said.
“When canals are filled, occupied or blocked by waste, the drainage system collapses. Restoring canals and protecting wetlands must become a priority if Dhaka wants to reduce waterlogging.”
Architect Iqbal Habib, an executive member of Bangladesh Poribesh Andolon, said every monsoon exposed the same failures of fragmented governance.
“This is not only about rainfall,” he said. “It is about blocking the natural flow of water through poor planning and weak coordination among government agencies.”
The two city corporations acknowledge the scale of the crisis.
Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Mohammad Shafiqul Islam Khan said years of accumulated waste and encroachment had left almost every canal in poor condition.
“If we fail to recover these canals, Dhaka cannot be protected,” he said, adding that the corporation planned to reclaim all 29 canals under its jurisdiction with public support.
Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Mohammad Abdus Salam blamed indiscriminate waste dumping and decades of unplanned development for the decline of canals and wetlands.
“People throw everything from polythene bags to pillows into drains,” he said.
He said the corporation planned to excavate canals in phases and restore natural drainage.
The investigation, however, indicates that the crisis cannot be attributed to public behaviour alone.
Rajuk has repeatedly faced criticism for failing to prevent developments that obstruct waterways and flood-flow zones.
Wasa’s infrastructure has been overwhelmed by illegal sewage connections.
The city corporations have struggled to remove encroachers and maintain canals regularly.
Environmental laws and court directives have also gone unenforced, allowing influential occupiers to retain control of public waterways.
The absence of a single accountable authority has enabled agencies to shift responsibility while the drainage system continues to deteriorate.
Urban planners warn that canal restoration is no longer merely an environmental or beautification exercise.
It has become essential to Dhaka’s survival as extreme rainfall and rapid construction place increasing pressure on the city.
Recovery would require more than periodically removing waste.
Authorities would have to demarcate canals, remove illegal structures, restore links between waterways and rivers, prevent sewage discharge, protect remaining wetlands and stop approving construction that blocks natural drainage.
Without those measures, experts say expensive pumping stations, underground drains and short-term clean-up drives will offer only temporary relief.
Dhaka was not built without an escape route for monsoon water.
The city had rivers, canals, wetlands and floodplains capable of carrying and absorbing it.
Those escape routes were systematically narrowed, polluted or buried.
As a result, Dhaka’s annual waterlogging is no longer an unavoidable natural disaster.
It is a man-made crisis resurfacing with every rainfall.

item.title: Health reform: 'We want to build a system, not just fix problems'
item.description:
Bangladesh's healthcare system has long faced staff shortages, weak governance, poor services, and widespread public dissatisfaction. The newly elected government has announced reforms including upgrading upazila health complexes to 101-bed hospitals, recruiting 5,000 doctors, improving hospital services, dismantling broker syndicates, ensuring doctor attendance, increasing procurement transparency, putting idle medical equipment into use, and strengthening immunization amid the ongoing measles outbreak.
How realistic are these plans? Can years of institutional decline be reversed? And when will quality healthcare reach people outside major cities?
In an interview with Dhaka Tribune Staff Reporter Tanvir Hasan, State Minister for Health and Family Planning Dr MA Muhit said the government's objective is not merely to solve immediate problems but to build an accountable, efficient healthcare system capable of delivering quality services nationwide.
Increasing bed capacity alone is not enough, and that is not our plan. As hospitals expand, staffing, equipment, logistics, and support systems must also grow.
Recruitment for 5,000 doctors has already begun, while additional doctors, nurses, midwives, and support staff will be appointed as new positions receive approval. Infrastructure development will take time, but planning is underway with technical input from doctors and engineers to ensure modern, sustainable facilities.
This is part of our broader commitment to strengthen the healthcare workforce through a phased approach where infrastructure, manpower, and logistics develop together.
Most of these problems were inherited. Equipment was often purchased without trained operators, installation planning, or maintenance, leaving costly machines idle.
Our approach is different. Procurement will be based on actual needs, and no equipment will be installed unless trained personnel are ready to operate it. Healthcare delivery—not procurement—must become the priority.
We also inherited weakened institutions. At Dhaka Medical College, for example, deteriorating hostel buildings now pose safety risks. That culture of neglect must end.
Since taking office, we have visited facilities from medical colleges to union-level health centres. Four major problems stand out: broker syndicates, absent doctors, shortages of essential medicines, and non-functional diagnostic equipment.
People simply want hospitals free from brokers, doctors present, medicines available, and functioning diagnostic services.
To improve security and discipline, every upazila health complex has been assigned 10 permanent Ansar personnel—nearly 5,000 nationwide. It will not solve every problem overnight, but it is an important first step, with additional measures under consideration.
Corruption is not unique to any institution. The real issue is weak systems.
Bangladesh needs institutions driven by systems rather than individuals. Technology can strengthen accountability by automatically identifying irregularities, much like AI-powered traffic monitoring. That is the direction we want to move toward.
Our field inspections and digital attendance records show the problem extends beyond rural areas.
In several Dhaka institutions, 40% to 50% of doctors posted there are not regularly present. Similar patterns exist in many upazilas, meaning absenteeism is a nationwide administrative problem rather than simply a rural one.
Today's upazilas are far better connected than in the past. The real issue is the collapse of accountability, where absenteeism carried few consequences for years.
That culture must change. Institutional discipline begins from the top, and we are committed to rebuilding a system where accountability is enforced consistently.
Before discussing 24-hour services, we must first restore the basics. In many hospitals, even daytime diagnostic services collapsed because equipment remained non-functional.
Our immediate goal is that every patient visiting a government hospital between 8am and 2pm can see a doctor, receive necessary tests, and obtain essential medicines. The healthcare system is still being rebuilt.
We do not believe in unrealistic promises. We are preparing a five-year healthcare reform roadmap with the Planning Ministry.
The first two years will focus on restoring basic healthcare, making institutions functional, and ensuring essential services. The following three years will expand and improve the system.
Upgrading upazila hospitals to 101 beds is central to that plan. Infrastructure work has already begun and will continue over the next 18 months alongside recruitment and institutional reforms.
From the third year onward, we aim to introduce 24-hour services, strengthen emergency care, improve security for healthcare workers, and make greater use of technology.
Our goal is to implement reforms step by step rather than make promises.
Procurement corruption has undoubtedly been a serious problem. However, the Ministry of Health oversees nearly 1,500 purchasing entities, with hospitals and medical colleges conducting procurement independently.
The issue is not decentralization but failure to follow existing procurement rules and the electronic Government Procurement system because of weak governance.
Our responsibility is to ensure those rules are followed transparently. Good governance depends on political commitment. Businesses should earn legitimate profits, but misuse of public funds must end.
During the government's first five months, neither the prime minister nor Cabinet members have faced major corruption allegations. People deserve a healthcare system where their taxes are spent properly.
Personally, I do not believe party politics belongs in professional organizations representing doctors or teachers.
Bangladesh has more than 100,000 registered doctors, including over 40,000 in government service. Compared with those numbers, DAB's membership is relatively small, and the perception that it controls the healthcare system is exaggerated.
Disagreements over appointments are inevitable across more than 1,500 healthcare institutions. What matters is how the government responds.
Where appointments were found to be inappropriate and legitimate objections were raised, we reversed those decisions. We are prepared to acknowledge mistakes and correct them.
I also welcome evidence-based criticism from the media. We are rebuilding a healthcare system that deteriorated over nearly two decades, and while mistakes may occur, they will be corrected.
The outbreak resulted from corruption under the previous government combined with later policy failures. Whether individuals are held accountable is a matter for the legal process, but my immediate priority is saving lives.
Following the outbreak, we held extensive consultations with EPI, surveillance teams, database managers, and immunization experts to assess vaccine demand.
We have completed month-by-month projections, placed procurement orders where shortages were identified, and introduced regular monitoring of vaccine stocks at both central and field levels. Based on current planning, Bangladesh has sufficient vaccine supplies for the coming year.
This is a serious concern. We found cases where children received the first dose but parents were never informed about subsequent doses.
We need greater public awareness so parents understand the vaccination schedule, alongside stronger accountability among healthcare workers.
Around 50,000 healthcare workers currently serve under the ministry, and another 100,000 will be recruited over the coming years. Both existing staff and new recruits will receive comprehensive training focused on immunization, accountability, professional responsibility, and service quality to ensure such failures do not happen again.
"Our goal is not simply to fix problems," Dr Muhit said. "We want to build a healthcare system that works—one that is accountable, efficient, and capable of delivering quality services to every citizen."

item.title: Senior journalist Kismat Khondokar dies; ERF mourns death
item.description:
Senior journalist and freedom fighter Khondokar Mohammad Abul Hasnat, widely known as Kismat Khondokar, died at a city hospital on Wednesday evening. He was 69.
Kismat Khondokar, a senior correspondent at online news portal Banglanews24.com and senior member of the Economic Reporters Forum (ERF), breathed his last at Nagorik Specialized Hospital in Jahurul Islam City (Aftabnagar) around 7:30pm, family sources said.
His nephew Risat said the journalist was staying at his sister’s house at Aftabnagar and was taken to the hospital after he fell ill, where he died.
According to the ERF, he will be buried at his village home in Mirzapur of Tangail district on Thursday.
Meanwhile, ERF President Doulot Akter Mala and General Secretary Abul Kashem expressed profound shock at Kismat Khondokar’s death.
In a condolence message, they prayed for eternal peace of the departed soul and conveyed heartfelt sympathy to the bereaved family.

item.title: Trump's special envoy Sergio Gor will arrive in Dhaka today
item.description:
US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor is scheduled to arrive in Dhaka today, Thursday afternoon for a three-day visit.

On the first day of his trip, Gor is expected to hold talks with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman.

Diplomatic sources said he is scheduled to visit Cox's Bazar on Friday to assess the situation of the Rohingya refugees firsthand.

Diplomats and international relations analysts view the visit as significant in light of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's recent trip to Beijing,

Bangladesh's growing engagement with various countries, and the latest regional diplomatic developments.

Gor is the third senior US official to visit Dhaka from Washington since the BNP government took office in February.

Earlier, Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs Paul Kapur visited Bangladesh in March, followed by Assistant US Trade Representative for South and Central Asia Brendan Lynch in May.

Trump’s special envoy due in Dhaka to sound out Bangladesh’s foreign policy direction

According to diplomatic sources, Gor's visit is expected to focus on Bangladesh's current foreign policy priorities, its strategic position in the region, and the future of Dhaka-Washington relations.

Washington's assessment of Bangladesh's evolving strategic role may also feature prominently in the discussions, particularly following the prime minister's visit to China in June, the foreign minister's trip to Moscow later that month, and the Turkish foreign minister's visit to Dhaka. If necessary, Gor may also convey messages from the administration of President Donald Trump to Bangladesh''s leadership.

President Donald Trump appointed businessman, politician and former White House official Sergio Gor as the US Special Envoy for South and Central Asia in August 2025.

Since assuming the role, he has emerged as one of the key figures in Washington's regional diplomacy.

In January this year, he began serving as the US ambassador to India.

Based in New Delhi, he is responsible for advancing US strategic relations not only with India but also with Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bhutan and other South Asian countries.

His visits to Nepal and Sri Lanka after taking up the envoy's role reflect that broader regional strategy.
